title: Abraham ibn Ezra
hookLine: traveler, poet, grammarian and sharp-eyed commentator

lines: CANDLES, AND THE SUN NEVER SETS.
A POET LAUGHS AT HIS LUCK.
cards: If I sold candles, the sun would never set. That's the gist of a short Hebrew poem, a joke a poet made about his own luck. If he dealt in burial shrouds, he goes on, nobody would die as long as he lived.
Whatever he tried, the world arranged itself so that he couldn't make a living. The man who wrote that was not a failure.
He was a sharp-eyed reader of the Bible, a grammarian, an astronomer, a poet, and a wanderer who carried his books from city to city. Today, Abraham ibn Ezra.

teach.b: Ibn Ezra grew up in Muslim Spain, in the world of the poets we've met this week. Then he left, and kept moving: Italy, France and, by his own writings, as far as England. Wherever he stayed, he wrote.
Spanish Jewish learning had grown up in Arabic, and Arabic was not the language of the Jews of Christian Europe. So ibn Ezra did something simple and huge: he wrote it out in Hebrew.
Grammar books, astronomy, and above all commentaries on the Bible.
As a commentator he wanted the plain meaning of the words, what Hebrew calls peshat. He paid close attention to grammar: how a verb is built, why a word is spelled the way it is.
He could be blunt with interpretations he thought ignored the words on the page. And he had a sharp eye for the odd detail.

teach.h: AND THE CANAANITE WAS THEN IN THE LAND.
teach.b: When Abram first arrives in the land, Genesis says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And the Canaanite was then in the land." Then? Ibn Ezra noticed that little word.
He wrote that there is a secret here, and that the one who understands it should keep silent. He doesn't say what the secret is.
Readers have argued ever since: some read it as a hint about who wrote that line and when; others read it differently. That's very ibn Ezra: sharp, brief, and willing to leave a question hanging.
A traveler learns to notice what locals stop seeing. Maybe that's why he saw so much in a word like then. He left behind commentaries that Jews still print beside the Torah.

how: Abraham ibn Ezra's commentary is printed alongside the Torah in editions of the Mikraot Gedolot, the rabbinic Bible, and students read him for his attention to grammar and plain meaning.

games.q: you are ibn Ezra reading Genesis: 'and the Canaanite was then in the land.' the word 'then' bothers you. what do you write?
o: a long essay explaining the answer.
that there is a secret here, and the wise keep silent.
games.why: he wrote that there is a secret, and the one who understands should keep silent, leaving the question hanging for readers ever since.

practice: Say the verse once, slowly: and the Canaanite was then in the land. Now read it the way ibn Ezra did: which word stops you, and what question would you write in the margin?
You don't need an answer; if you pray, you can ask in your own words to read with open eyes.
